title: Cloud Computing: An Overview
topics: AI and Big Data in Cloud

bullets.text: Lecture will cover meaning, features, models, advantages, challenges, and applications of cloud computing.
Defined as the delivery of computing services (servers, storage, databases, software, AI) over the internet.
It is a way of renting computing resources instead of buying and maintaining them locally.
Analogy: paying for electricity without owning the power plant, only for consumption.
This model makes technology more affordable, scalable, and convenient.
On-demand self-service: users access resources as needed without human interaction.
Broad network access: services are available over the internet from various devices.
Resource pooling: providers share resources across multiple customers while keeping data isolated.
Rapid elasticity: resources can scale up or down quickly based on demand.
Measured service: usage is monitored and billed according to resources consumed.
Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS): delivers fundamental computing resources like virtual machines, storage, and networking (e.g., Amazon Web Services EC2).
Platform as a Service (PaaS): provides infrastructure plus a development platform with built-in tools and frameworks (e.g., Google App Engine).
Software as a Service (SaaS): delivers ready-to-use applications over the internet, accessed via a browser (e.g., Gmail, Microsoft 365, Zoom).
Public Cloud: services delivered over the internet, shared by multiple organizations, cost-effective but may raise security concerns.
Private Cloud: dedicated to a single organization, offering more control and security but potentially more expensive.
Hybrid Cloud: combines public and private clouds to balance flexibility with security.
Community Cloud: shared by several organizations with common goals or requirements (e.g., healthcare, education).

sections.heading: Advantages and Challenges of Cloud Computing

bullets.text: Advantages include reduced costs, improved scalability, enhanced flexibility, increased reliability, and support for innovation.
Challenges involve security and privacy concerns due to data stored on remote servers.
Downtime: internet connectivity issues can affect access to critical resources.
Compliance: strict regulations in certain industries regarding data storage.
Vendor lock-in: difficulty and cost associated with switching cloud providers.
Performance concerns for applications requiring very high processing speed or low latency.
Data storage and backup (e.g., Google Drive, Dropbox, OneDrive).
Business collaboration tools (e.g., Slack, Microsoft Teams).
Entertainment streaming platforms (e.g., Netflix, Spotify).
Healthcare solutions (e.g., electronic medical records, telemedicine).
Education platforms (e.g., Coursera, Google Classroom).
Research for large-scale data analysis, machine learning, and AI projects.
Cloud computing is crucial for AI and big data analytics, providing high-performance computing resources on demand.
Edge computing processes data closer to the source, reducing latency, but still relies on the cloud for management.
Future trends include multi-cloud strategies to avoid vendor lock-in and improve reliability.
Serverless computing allows developers to focus on code, with the provider managing infrastructure automatically.
Continued focus on security, compliance, and integration with AI, blockchain, and 5G technologies.
